extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and practitioners of digital/media culture; content creators interested in viral/memetic success
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the textual, visual, and social features that make online videos and photos likely to be shared, imitated, or remixed (i.e., go viral or become memetic), and to classify common meme genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic content that is clearly intended to be humorous and intertwined with play; humor enjoyed for its own sake and involving multilayered perception of social situations (drawing on Huizinga's Homo ludens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playfulness can lure user creativity by summoning viewers to take part in a game; playful texts invite participation and imitation. Examples: explicitly humorous user-created clips; play/performance modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy deriving from an unexpected cognitive encounter between two incongruent elements (e.g., a pun, a man in women’s clothing, or a dancing banana).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audio–visual incongruity is especially salient (e.g., lipsynch, contrast between appearance and voice). This multimodal dissonance creates puzzles users may try to solve or highlight by creating variants. Examples: 'Numa Numa' (lipsynch), 'Chocolate Rain' (boyish appearance vs mature voice), 'Charlie Bit My Finger' (sound vs observed action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor associated with feelings of one-upmanship: laughter as pleasurable expression of perceived superiority over others (classical superiority theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unintentionally funny subjects (people acting awkwardly) can trigger remakes and mocking imitations that publicly demonstrate imitators' superiority. Examples: 'David after Dentist,' 'Star Wars Kid,' 'Miss Teenage South Carolina'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveying one uncomplicated idea or slogan; simple visual construction (one or two performers), often filmed in one take or single shot, plain backgrounds or domestic settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity enables easy imitation by average users with limited resources and low digital literacy. Professional clips that include simple, repeated elements can also be memetic. Examples: 'Leave Britney Alone', 'Numa Numa', 'Evolution of Dance', some sequences in 'Single Ladies'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporation of a single simple unit that is repeated throughout the clip (lyrics, movement, line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition demonstrates replicability and enhances memorability, both of which encourage imitation and remakes. It embeds 'encrypted instructions' for replication. Examples: 'Chocolate Rain' lyrics/melody, 'Peanut Butter Jelly Time' banana, 'Put a ring on it' in 'Single Ladies'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whimsical Content / Lack of Concrete Theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency toward whimsical, playful, or non-concrete subject matter rather than polarizing themes (politics, religion, sex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing popular culture (non-polarizing) and whimsical presentation reduce alienation of audience and make imitation easier; playfulness plus lack of concrete content allows imitators to inject personal themes. Examples: 'Zombie Kid', 'Charlie Bit My Finger'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Ordinary People
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ordinary, non-celebrity protagonists rather than polished celebrity performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary people make texts feel incomplete or flawed and thus invite user participation and replication (producerly texts). This contrasts with visually rich celebrity content which tends not to generate derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flawed Masculinity (as a memetic trait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of 'flawed', atypical, or exaggerated masculinity (e.g., awkward or non-conforming male performers) as a recurrent memetic attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flawed masculinity makes performers stand out and can increase memetic potential by making content feel quirky or mockable (example discussion: PSY as a 'weird bird' in K-pop).

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual Incompleteness / Amateur-looking Aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos that appear unfinished, unpolished, amateur, or weird—textually incomplete or flawed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incompleteness invites users to fill gaps, address puzzles, or mock creators, enhancing spreadability and the tendency to produce derivatives. Tied to Jenkins' and Fiske's notions of 'gaps' and 'producerly texts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image Juxtaposition (memetic photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Striking incongruity between two or more elements in a photograph where one person sticks out as alien to the surrounding situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juxtapositions provoke Photoshop-based memetic responses either by deepening ridicule (placing the subject in even stronger incongruent scenarios) or diminishing it (repositioning the subject into fitting contexts). Examples: 'Disaster Girl', 'Frowning Flower Girl'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen Motion (memetic photos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs that capture people mid-action—an intense movement 'frozen in time'—often resulting in ungainly or ludicrous postures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 'still moving' images invite users to 'join the action' and complete an apparently unfinished movement; they generate memetic reactions due to instability/absurdity. Examples: 'Bubble Girl', 'Leonardo DiHapprio' images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple Packaging (viral & memetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, quickly comprehensible packaging of content so viewers understand it intuitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple packaging enhances sharing (viral) because it is easy to forward and enhances memetic responses because it is easy to imitate. Apply to both videos and photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor / Positive Valence (viral & memetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of humor or broadly positive valence that makes people want to amuse friends and be associated with wittiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor increases both forwarding (virality) and the tendency to remake/imitate (memetic), via playfulness, incongruity, and superiority feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augmented Participation Tools (viral & memetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision of tools or action points (beyond mere content diffusion) that enable users to participate, modify, or act on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation tools deepen users' sense of agency and involvement, promoting sharing and often causing content to transition from 'viral' to 'memetic' as users reappropriate and personalize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige (viral-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Association with status, celebrity, or professionally produced elements that confer prestige on the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige drives sharing in ways similar to mass-media success (e.g., flashy stars increase likelihood of success); prestige is more relevant for virality than for memetic replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positioning (viral-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic placement or timing of content (e.g., prime-time placement, high-visibility channels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning matters for reach and initial uptake (akin to broadcast scheduling); important for viral success but less central to memetic imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provocation of Strong Emotions (viral-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that provokes strong emotions (e.g., outrage, awe, deep inspiration) which motivate people to share as expressions of their own stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong emotional arousal fuels forwarding behavior; relevant for viral spread even when content is not easily imitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifesting Memetic Potential (memetic-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs within the content that demonstrate its replicability—e.g., repetition in videos or a Photoshopped-like appearance in photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit demonstrators of replicability (repetition, easily copied elements, or already 'Photoshopped' look) encourage creative remixes and derivatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puzzle / Problem Introduction (memetic-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding a puzzle, dissonance, or problem (often via incongruity) that invites users to creatively respond or 'solve' it through remixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puzzles stimulate creative participation and memetic responses by giving users something to address—either by explaining, extending, or resolving the incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meme Literacy Level (genre-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different meme genres require different levels of cultural and technical literacy—some can be understood/created by almost anyone, others require detailed subcultural knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience's meme literacy when creating or evaluating memes; low-literacy-friendly genres drive broad participation, high-literacy genres circulate within subcultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction Photoshops (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Images created in response to memetic photos (Photoshop-based variants of an original that place the subject in alternate contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaction Photoshops capitalize on the original photo's incongruity; they're iterative and often numerous (e.g., 'Tourist Guy' edited into many historical scenes). Useful as a production template for memetic photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photo Fads (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Staged photos of people imitating specific positions or actions in various settings intended for posting (e.g., planking, 'heads in freezers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photo fads are easy to reproduce en masse and rely on simple, recognizable poses; they function like performative templates for participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash Mob (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinated gatherings where strangers perform a public act suddenly and leave; organized via internet/mobile and then photographed/posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash mobs can be apolitical or carry anticonsumerist framing; they require coordination and may be coopted for commercial PR (which can subvert original genre values). Historical/genre roots in avant-garde prank traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lipsynch / Lipdub (genre definition and subgenres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos of individuals or groups matching lip movements to a song; includes 'bedroom lipsynchs' (small, webcam-based, private) and 'collective lipdubs' (large, organization-based, filmed in one continuous shot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bedroom lipdubs emphasize individual presence and are easy to produce; collective lipdubs are organizational and often serve PR purposes. Both reappropriate mass-media hits and blend fame/anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misheard Lyrics / Phonetic Translation (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Videos that transcribe audio phonetically to create amusing mistranslations (animutations, 'buffalax' style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rely on cross-linguistic phonetic resemblance and subtitle insertion; they became a distinct genre via examples like 'Benny Lava' and animate playful mistranslations across language pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recut Trailers (genre definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: User-created 'fake' movie trailers made by re-editing film footage to displace the original genre or tone (e.g., turning horror into comedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recuts parody marketing strategies and reflect audience familiarity with trailer formulas; they also serve as demonstrations of creators' digital literacy and critique advertising mechanics.
